content: 1. Drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol/levomefolate calcium and levomefolate calcium is a combination contraceptive approved by the FDA for preventing pregnancy, managing premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), treating acne, and providing folate supplementation. 2. This medication carries a Black Box Warning, indicating significant risks associated with its use. 3. Common adverse reactions include weight gain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, depression, irritability, mood swings, breakthrough bleeding, breast tenderness, menstrual irregularities, breast pain, reduced libido, and fatigue. 4. The recommended dosage for adults is one tablet taken orally once daily at the same time each day. 5. Missing pills or taking them incorrectly can increase the failure rate of the medication. 6. To maximize contraceptive and PMDD effectiveness, the medication must be taken as directed, in the order specified on the blister pack. 7. If a single pill is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered. 8. Patients can start the medication on the first day of their menstrual period (Day 1 Start) or the first Sunday after the onset of their period (Sunday Start). 9. For a Day 1 Start, the patient should take one pink tablet daily for 24 consecutive days, followed by one light orange tablet daily on Days 25 through 28. 10. The medication should be taken in the order directed on the package, preferably after the evening meal or at bedtime with some liquid, if needed. 11. Drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol/levomefolate calcium can be taken with or without food. 12. If the medication is started later than the first day of the menstrual cycle, it should not be considered effective as a contraceptive until after seven consecutive days of administration. 13. Patients should use a non-hormonal contraceptive as a backup during the first seven days of starting the medication. 14. The possibility of ovulation and conception prior to initiating the medication should be considered. 15. For a Sunday Start, the patient should take one pink tablet daily beginning on the first Sunday after the onset of her menstrual period, followed by one light orange tablet daily on Days 25 through 28. 16. The patient should begin her next and all subsequent 28-day regimens on the same day of the week that she began her first regimen, following the same schedule. 17. If a subsequent cycle is started later than the day following the last light orange tablet, the patient should use another method of contraception until she has taken a pink tablet daily for seven consecutive days. 18. When switching from another birth control pill, start this medication on the same day a new pack of the previous oral contraceptive would have been started. 19. When switching from a transdermal patch or vaginal ring, start this medication when the next application would have been due. 20. When switching from an injection, start this medication when the next dose would have been due. 21. When switching from an intrauterine contraceptive or implant, start this medication on the day of removal. 22. Withdrawal bleeding usually occurs within three days following the last pink tablet. 23. If spotting or breakthrough bleeding occurs, the patient should continue taking the medication as directed. This type of bleeding is usually transient and without significance, but persistent or prolonged bleeding should prompt consultation with a healthcare provider. 24. If withdrawal bleeding does not occur, consider the possibility of pregnancy. 25. 26. If the patient has adhered to the prescribed regimen and misses two consecutive periods, rule out pregnancy. 27. Discontinue the medication if pregnancy is confirmed. 28. The risk of pregnancy increases with each active pink tablet missed. 29. For postpartum women who do not breastfeed or after a second-trimester abortion, start the medication no earlier than four weeks postpartum due to the increased risk of thromboembolism. 30. If the patient starts the medication postpartum and has not yet had a period, evaluate for possible pregnancy and instruct her to use an additional method of contraception until she has taken the medication for seven consecutive days. 31. 32. If vomiting occurs within 3-4 hours after taking a tablet, it can be regarded as a missed tablet. 33. Women of childbearing age are recommended to consume supplemental folic acid at a dose of at least 0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily. 34. Consider other folate supplementation a woman may be taking before prescribing this medication. 35. 36. There is limited information regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use of this medication in adult or pediatric patients. 37. Safety and efficacy have been established in women of reproductive age, and efficacy is expected to be the same for postpubertal adolescents under 18 and users 18 years and older. Use before menarche is not indicated. 38. Do not prescribe this medication to women with renal impairment, adrenal insufficiency, a high risk of arterial or venous thrombotic diseases, or other contraindications such as smoking over age 35, uncontrolled hypertension, or certain cancers. 39. Stop the medication if an arterial or venous thrombotic event occurs. 40. Drospirenone-containing contraceptives may be associated with a higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) compared to other contraceptives. 41. Known risk factors for VTE include smoking, obesity, and a family history of VTE. 42. The risk of VTE is highest during the first year of use and gradually decreases after discontinuation of the medication. 43. Use of combined oral contraceptives (COCs) also increases the risk of arterial thromboses such as strokes and myocardial infarctions, especially in women with other risk factors. 44. Women with cardiovascular disease risk factors should use COCs with caution. 45. Stop the medication if there is unexplained loss of vision, proptosis, diplopia, papilledema, or retinal vascular lesions, and evaluate for retinal vein thrombosis immediately. 46. This medication contains drospirenone, which has antimineralocorticoid activity and may cause hyperkalemia in high-risk patients. 47. Women with conditions predisposing to hyperkalemia, such as renal impairment, hepatic impairment, or adrenal insufficiency, should not use this medication. 48. Women on long-term treatment with medications that may increase serum potassium should have their potassium levels checked during the first treatment cycle. 49. Women with a history of breast cancer or other estrogenor progestin-sensitive cancers should not use this medication. 50. Discontinue the medication if jaundice develops or if liver function is impaired. 51. Women with a history of COC-related cholestasis may have the condition recur with subsequent COC use. 52. 53. Women with uncontrolled hypertension or hypertension with vascular disease should not use COCs. 54. Studies suggest a small increased risk of gallbladder disease among COC users. 55. Monitor prediabetic and diabetic women carefully, as COCs may decrease glucose tolerance. 56. Women with hypertriglyceridemia or a family history of it may be at increased risk of pancreatitis when using COCs. 57. If a woman develops new, recurrent, persistent, or severe headaches, evaluate the cause and discontinue the medication if indicated. 58. Unscheduled bleeding or spotting may occur, especially during the first three months of use. Persistent or irregular bleeding should prompt evaluation for pregnancy or malignancy. 59. Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives prior to pregnancy. 60. Discontinue the medication if pregnancy is confirmed and initiate a prenatal vitamin containing folate supplementation. 61. Women with a history of depression should be carefully observed, and the medication should be discontinued if depression recurs to a serious degree. 62. The use of COCs may change the results of some laboratory tests.
